A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cognitive-modeling project. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching v1’s synthetic experiments to v2’s Appendices C–D.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic decision-making and learning experiments, plus model-fitting analyses of human bandit-task data in Sections 3–5.

after.justification: V2 reports original model-fitting and predictive-check results across four cognitive domains, additional control analyses, and the retained synthetic experiments.

M1.justification: The three-model, ten-iteration guided search, optimization and feedback mechanism are retained under the GeCCo name. A limited procedural change concerns initialization: v1 specifies a counterfactual-learning template for human full-feedback learning, whereas v2 Appendix B.2 supplies a two-rate RW template that updates only chosen-action values.

E1.justification: V2 retains the synthetic tasks and both human learning conditions, while adding human multi-attribute decisions from Hilbig and Moshagen, two-stage planning from Feher da Silva and Hare, and reinforcement-learning–working-memory data from Rmus et al. These introduce feature validities, multistage transitions and varying memory loads.

E2.justification: V2 evaluates pWADD, Hybrid and RL–WM baselines in the new human tasks and adds CENTAUR comparisons in Table 1. Within retained human-learning comparisons, v1’s vanilla RW and simple counterfactual controls disappear; the winning two-rate and four-rate RW models remain.

E3.justification: The expanded experiments introduce R1 and Qwen configurations, with temperatures 0.1 and 0.15, exceedance probabilities alongside BIC, NLL-based comparison with CENTAUR, and domain-specific human predictive-check procedures. The original BIC criterion, 20 optimizer initializations and Llama generation temperature remain.

E4.justification: V2 adds prompt-component ablations, LLM-feature analyses, LogProber contamination checks, convergence curves and human posterior predictive checks. The original noise tests and principal synthetic recovery analyses are retained. V1’s separate cumulative-reward check and winning-template control in Appendices B–C are removed.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports five independent complete GeCCo runs per domain and SEM across these runs in Figure 11, distinct from the retained ten sampling iterations. It also adds mixed-effects regressions and exceedance probabilities. V1 already reported SEM, t-tests and repeated heuristic experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive human-task, multi-LLM and control results. Its full-feedback comparison reports LLM/baseline BICs of 77.97/85.24, versus 78.74/78.19 in v1. Generated models differ and identical evaluation subsets are not established, so these are not direct version-to-version performance gains. Principal synthetic accuracy and recovery values remain unchanged in Appendices C–D.

T1.justification: Appendix F adds formal definitions for feature-weighted decision rules, hybrid planning updates and RL–WM mixture policies absent from v1. The original RW mathematics is retained in Appendix D. This expands mathematical specification without introducing new proofs or theoretical guarantees.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from demonstrating model identification and generation to presenting GeCCo as a general model-generation pipeline matching or surpassing literature models across four human domains. V2 additionally claims explanatory-variance coverage comparable to CENTAUR and identifies prompt feedback and reasoning as performance drivers.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning parsimonious heuristic selection, counterfactual learning mechanisms, transition-sensitive planning and the localization of memory-load effects. It also interprets the control analyses and expands discussion of template bias, participant-specific structures and naturalistic-data limitations. These go beyond v1’s general discussion of novelty, prompting and domain coverage.

D1.justification: V2 provides human-task prompts and templates, model-specific settings, GPU/runtime information and ChatGPT-assisted simulation details. It newly distinguishes training, validation and test data, although split sizes remain unspecified. Conversely, it removes v1’s parser and model-identification listings and explicit synthetic-parameter sampling ranges.

R1.justification: The model-discovery and program-synthesis positioning remains. V2 adds discussion of concurrent cognitive-model discovery by Xie et al. and Castro et al., claims faster convergence, and introduces literature supporting the added domains and mechanistic interpretations.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title, introduces GeCCo terminology, substantially rewrites the abstract and narrative, consolidates methods, and organizes the main text around four human domains. Synthetic experiments move to appendices, partial-feedback results move to Appendix G, and related work moves into the discussion.

P2.justification: The pipeline schematic is redrawn, and human-result figures now combine task schematics, model comparisons, predictive checks and code. V2 adds prompt, ablation, contamination and convergence displays plus the CENTAUR table. V1 Figures 2–3 and Table 1 are relocated, while its supplementary Figures 5–6 disappear.

improvement.justification: V1’s broad applicability claim rests mainly on simple simulations and one human bandit study. V2 tests that claim on three additional human paradigms and adds component ablations, repeated-run variability and human predictive checks, substantially strengthening validation. These gains outweigh the loss of some earlier reproducibility details. Important overinterpretations remain: the reported reasoning effect is not significant, and CENTAUR is only a proxy for an explainable-variance ceiling (Section 7; Table 1).
